name: The Bottle of the Ifrit
powers: Held a vast ifrit imprisoned for centuries until a fisherman freed him.
description: The sealed copper bottle cast up in the fisherman's net in the Thousand and One Nights tale of the Fisherman and the Jinni, from which a vast ifrit escaped in a pillar of smoke and threatened to kill his liberator. The fisherman tricked the spirit back into the vessel by doubting that so great a being could fit. The jar is the archetype of the bottled-jinn motif in world folklore.
source: Thousand and One Nights, The Fisherman and the Jinni

name: Inukshuk
powers: Guides travelers and marks the good hunting ground.
description: Figures built of stacked stones by Inuit and other Arctic peoples, used as landmarks to guide travelers, mark good hunting or fishing places, or stand as memorials on the open tundra where there are no trees. The human-shaped inuksuk is best known from the flag of Nunavut, though most cairns were simple and practical. Each is a deliberate sign in a landscape that offers few bearings.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Iara's Hair
material: None (a physical feature of the spirit)
era: Brazilian folk tradition to the present
powers: Her combed hair lures lovers into the river's depths.
description: The long dark hair that the Iara combs while singing at the riverbank, her voice and beauty drawing young men to drown in her waters; the hair and the combing are the heart of her image in Brazilian legend. Rooted in river tales and blended with the water spirit of the Tupi peoples, she appears as the enchantress of the deep. The comb she keeps is said to hold the charm of her voice.
